topic: How the label for a difficulty shapes how serious it feels
text:
How we name a difficulty may shape how serious it feels. In an Australian randomised online trial, 676 adults imagined telling their GP they had been exhausted, sleeping poorly and pulling back from people at work. Being told it was depression led people to rate the situation as more serious than being told it was burnout, a made-up label or no label at all. Yet the label made no clear difference to their intention to seek help or to stigma.

Why this matters across roles: whether you are a GP, psychologist, counsellor or support worker, the words used for a difficulty can change how serious it feels to the person hearing them.

One practical takeaway: when you name a difficulty, check what that word means to the person, and give them room to say how it lands.

Where the evidence stops:
• Participants imagined a scenario, and the study measured intention, not actual help-seeking.
• The scenario described milder difficulties in a work setting, so results may differ for more intense experiences.
• Data were collected during the COVID-19 pandemic, which may have shaped attitudes.

Key source: Smith et al., 2023: https://doi.org/10.1002/jclp.23410
